implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines makes the two phases explicit through the Job lifecycle: cancel() is phase 1 and, as the docs put it, cancelling does not mean the computation finishes immediately - cancellation is cooperative and observed at the next suspension point - while join()/cancelAndJoin() is phase 2. Cleanup runs in a finally block wrapped in withContext(NonCancellable), because otherwise the cleanup itself is cut short by the very cancellation it is responding to, and structured concurrency means a scope completes only after all children complete, so joining the scope doubles as the completion signal. Hand-rolled java.lang.Thread workers still need the JVM flag/interrupt/join form; the classic latch structure disappears because the Job already models requested-versus-completed.
pitfalls: cancel() is only a request: a coroutine blocked in non-suspending code or a blocking call (Thread.sleep, a JDBC driver) never reaches a safe point, so such work must be moved to suspending APIs or guarded with ensureActive().

Cleanup that suspends after cancellation throws CancellationException at its first suspension unless it is inside withContext(NonCancellable) - without it the flush never happens, which is the most common corrupted-shutdown bug in coroutine code.

Never launch children inside a NonCancellable block: the parent-child relation is severed, so the parent neither waits for them nor propagates failure; wrap them in coroutineScope inside the NonCancellable block if you need child work.
Cancelling a child with a plain Job inside a regular scope cancels its parent (transparency), which can shut down more than intended; use SupervisorJob when children must stop independently.
